title: Κεραυνὸς πρόσθ’ ἵππων
titleEn: The Thunderbolt Before the Horses — Iliad 8.97–197
about: Odysseus runs past Diomedes’ call without a word, and Diomedes goes alone to the front, where he stops before Nestor’s horses and offers the old man his own chariot, drawn by the Trojan horses he once took from Aeneas. Nestor takes the reins; Diomedes throws his spear at Hector and kills his charioteer Eniopeus instead. Hector finds a new driver, and the Trojans would have been penned in Troy like lambs had Zeus not hurled a thunderbolt in front of Diomedes’ horses. Nestor, frightened, tells Diomedes to turn back and says that Zeus is giving the glory to Hector today. Diomedes does not want to hear Hector say that he fled, but Nestor answers that the Trojans would not believe such a charge. Hector shouts taunts at Diomedes’ back, and Diomedes wavers three times, and Zeus thunders three times from Ida for the Trojans. Hector rallies his men, mocks the Achaean wall, and calls on his horses by name to catch Nestor’s shield and Diomedes’ breastplate.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἐσάκουσε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἀλλὰ παρήϊξεν κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, nor did he listen, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
but rushed past to the hollow ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: So he spoke, but much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus did not listen, and rushed past to the hollow ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: Odysseus does not answer Diomedes’ call for help (the last words of his speech are in the previous part); he simply runs on past. ὣς ἔφατ’ is the stock closing of a speech, ἔφατ’ being ἔφατο with the vowel cut off, and οὐδ’ is οὐδέ ‘and not’. ἐσάκουσε is the aorist of ἐσακούω (Attic εἰσακούω) ‘listen to, heed’, and παρήϊξεν is παρά + ἀΐσσω ‘dart’, so ‘rushed past’. The reason for his silence is not given. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδης δ’ αὐτός περ ἐὼν προμάχοισιν ἐμίχθη,
στῆ δὲ πρόσθ’ ἵππων Νηληϊάδαο γέροντος,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And Tydeus’-son, himself though he was, mingled with the front-fighters,
and stood in front of the horses of the old man, Neleus’-son,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Though he was alone, the son of Tydeus mingled with the foremost fighters, and stood in front of the horses of the old man, the son of Neleus, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: Diomedes is the subject (Τυδεΐδης, ‘son of Tydeus’) and the old man is Nestor, not yet named: Νηληϊάδαο is a patronymic, ‘son of Neleus’, with the epic genitive ending -αο. αὐτός περ ἐών means ‘though being himself’, that is, by himself, with no one beside him. προμάχοισιν ἐμίχθη is ‘mingled with the foremost fighters’. The last line is the stock introduction, with μιν ‘him’ (Nestor) and φωνήσας ‘lifting his voice’; ἔπεα πτερόεντα are ‘winged words’, the speech that follows.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον ἦ μάλα δή σε νέοι τείρουσι μαχηταί,
σὴ δὲ βίη λέλυται, χαλεπὸν δέ σε γῆρας ὀπάζει,
sentences.l:
“O old man, truly, very much do young fighters wear you down,
and your strength is loosed, and harsh old age attends you,
sentences.i: “Old man, young fighters are wearing you down hard indeed; your strength has slackened, and harsh old age is upon you,
sentences.n: Diomedes’ offer to Nestor begins with the facts of his age. ὦ γέρον is ‘old man’, and ἦ μάλα δή is a strong particle group, ‘truly, very much’. τείρουσι is ‘wear down’. λέλυται is the perfect passive of λύω, ‘has been loosed’, so the strength lies slack; σὴ … βίη is ‘your strength’. ὀπάζει means ‘makes follow, attends’: old age is always at his side. Diomedes’ speech begins.

sentences.t: ἠπεδανὸς δέ νύ τοι θεράπων, βραδέες δέ τοι ἵπποι.
sentences.l: and weak is your attendant, and slow are your horses.
sentences.i: your attendant is feeble, and your horses are slow.
sentences.n: Two more reasons Nestor cannot keep up. ἠπεδανός is a rare word, taken to mean ‘infirm, feeble’; its origin is not certain. θεράπων ‘attendant’ is Nestor’s own man. βραδέες is the epic plural of βραδύς ‘slow’, and νύ … τοι is ‘you see, to you’. The line holds two short clauses with no verb, ‘is’ being understood.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ἐμῶν ὀχέων ἐπιβήσεο, ὄφρα ἴδηαι
οἷοι Τρώϊοι ἵπποι ἐπιστάμενοι πεδίοιο
κραιπνὰ μάλ’ ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα διωκέμεν ἠδὲ φέβεσθαι,
οὕς ποτ’ ἀπ’ Αἰνείαν ἑλόμην μήστωρε φόβοιο.
sentences.l:
But come, mount my chariot, so that you may see
what sort the Trojan horses are, knowing how, over the plain,
very much in a rush, this way and that to pursue and to flee,
those that once from Aeneas I took, counsellors of flight.
sentences.i: But come, mount my chariot, and you will see what sort of horses the Trojans have, how well they know how to rush this way and that over the plain, in pursuit or in flight, the horses I once took from Aeneas, masters of flight.
sentences.n: Diomedes invites Nestor into his own chariot. ὀχέων ἐπιβήσεο is ‘mount the chariot’ (ἐπιβαίνω takes the genitive), a middle imperative. ὄφρα ἴδηαι is a purpose clause with the epic subjunctive ‘you may see’. ἐπιστάμενοι ‘knowing how’ governs the infinitives διωκέμεν ‘to pursue’ and φέβεσθαι ‘to flee’ (epic -μεν for -ειν). ἀπ’ … ἑλόμην is ἀφελόμην with the preposition split from the verb, ‘I took from’, and Αἰνείαν is the epic accusative ‘Aeneas’. μήστωρε is a dual (‘the two’) and φόβοιο is the genitive of φόβος ‘flight’, so the horses are ‘counsellors’ in the work of flight, that is, masters of it.

sentences.t:
τούτω μὲν θεράποντε κομείτων, τώδε δὲ νῶϊ
Τρωσὶν ἐφ’ ἱπποδάμοις ἰθύνομεν,
sentences.l:
These two let the two attendants tend, and these two let us two
steer straight against the horse-taming Trojans,
sentences.i: Let the two attendants tend these two, and let us two drive these two straight at the Trojans, tamers of horses,
sentences.n: The speech is full of duals, the Greek form for pairs: τούτω ‘these two’ (Nestor’s horses, as 113 shows), θεράποντε ‘two attendants’, κομείτων ‘let them two tend’, τώδε ‘these two’ (the Trojan horses just praised), and νῶϊ ‘we two’, Diomedes and Nestor. ἰθύνομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive used as an exhortation, ‘let us steer’, from ἰθύνω ‘make straight’. ἐφ’ … Τρωσὶν is ἐπὶ Τρωσίν ‘at the Trojans’, and ἱπποδάμοις ‘horse-taming’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα καὶ Ἕκτωρ
εἴσεται εἰ καὶ ἐμὸν δόρυ μαίνεται ἐν παλάμῃσιν.
sentences.l:
so that Hector too
will know whether my spear also rages in my palms.”
sentences.i: so that Hector too will know whether my spear also rages in my hands.”
sentences.n: The purpose of the plan is to let Hector learn what Diomedes can do. ὄφρα with the future εἴσεται (from οἶδα) means ‘so that he will know’, and εἰ … μαίνεται is an indirect question, ‘whether it rages’: the spear is said to rage like a man in a frenzy. παλάμῃσιν is the epic dative plural ‘palms’, that is, hands. Diomedes’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and did not disobey, the Gerenian horseman Nestor;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the Gerenian horseman Nestor did not disobey him;
sentences.n: Nestor’s name arrives with his standing epithet. οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε is ‘and did not disobey’ (ἀπιθέω, the opposite of πείθομαι ‘obey’). Γερήνιος ἱππότα is ‘Gerenian horseman’; the meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed (Gerenia or Gerenon, a place in Messenia, or a word connected with γέρων ‘old man’ or γέρας), and ἱππότα is the epic nominative of ἱππότης, with a long -α. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
Νεστορέας μὲν ἔπειθ’ ἵππους θεράποντε κομείτην
ἴφθιμοι Σθένελός τε καὶ Εὐρυμέδων ἀγαπήνωρ.
sentences.l:
Then Nestor’s horses the two attendants tended,
mighty Sthenelus and Eurymedon, man-cherishing.
sentences.i: Then mighty Sthenelus and Eurymedon, who prized manliness, tended Nestor’s horses as his two attendants.
sentences.n: The μέν in Νεστορέας μέν is answered by τὼ δέ in the next line: Nestor’s horses go to the attendants, and the two chiefs mount Diomedes’ chariot. Νεστορέας is an adjective, ‘of Nestor’, and κομείτην is the dual of the past tense of κομέω ‘tend’. ἴφθιμοι ‘mighty’ agrees with the two names. ἀγαπήνωρ is from ἀγαπάω + ἀνήρ and its exact sense is not known (‘prizing manliness’ is one guess).

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ εἰς ἀμφοτέρω Διομήδεος ἅρματα βήτην·
sentences.l: and the two, both, into Diomedes’ chariot went;
sentences.i: and the two of them both stepped into Diomedes’ chariot;
sentences.n: τὼ … ἀμφοτέρω ‘the two, both’ are Nestor and Diomedes, a dual noun group. βήτην is the dual of the aorist ἔβην (ἔβητην) ‘went’, here ‘stepped’. ἅρματα is a neuter plural but is used of a single chariot.

sentences.t:
Νέστωρ δ’ ἐν χείρεσσι λάβ’ ἡνία σιγαλόεντα,
μάστιξεν δ’ ἵππους·
sentences.l:
and Nestor in his hands took the glossy reins,
and whipped the horses;
sentences.i: and Nestor took the glossy reins in his hands and whipped the horses;
sentences.n: It is Nestor who drives, so the reins pass to him. λάβ’ is ἔλαβε with the vowel elided and without the augment, ‘took’, and ἡνία σιγαλόεντα are ‘glossy reins’. μάστιξεν is the aorist of μαστίζω ‘whip’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: τάχα δ’ Ἕκτορος ἄγχι γένοντο.
sentences.l: and soon near Hector they came.
sentences.i: and soon they were near Hector.
sentences.n: τάχα ‘soon, quickly’ and ἄγχι ‘near’ (with the genitive Ἕκτορος) tell how fast the chariot goes. γένοντο is the aorist of γίγνομαι, ‘came to be’, with the unaugmented plural form of the poet’s past tenses.

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ ἰθὺς μεμαῶτος ἀκόντισε Τυδέος υἱός·
sentences.l: and at him, straight, eager as he was, cast the son of Tydeus;
sentences.i: and the son of Tydeus cast his spear straight at him, eager as he was;
sentences.n: The subject Τυδέος υἱός comes last. τοῦ is Hector, and τοῦ … μεμαῶτος is a genitive ‘as he was eager’ (μεμαώς, perfect participle of μάω, ‘eager’), a word the poet uses of a man rushing forward. ἰθύς is ‘straight’. ἀκόντισε is ‘cast’ (ἀκοντίζω); the Greek gives no object, and ‘his spear’ is supplied. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: καὶ τοῦ μέν ῥ’ ἀφάμαρτεν,
sentences.l: and him indeed he missed,
sentences.i: and him he missed,
sentences.n: μέν ῥ’ is μὲν ῥα, with ῥ’ the particle ῥα, ‘indeed, as it happened’, and the μέν is answered by ὃ δέ in the next line. τοῦ is Hector again; ἀφάμαρτεν is the aorist of ἀφαμαρτάνω ‘miss’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἡνίοχον θεράποντα
υἱὸν ὑπερθύμου Θηβαίου Ἠνιοπῆα
ἵππων ἡνί’ ἔχοντα βάλε στῆθος παρὰ μαζόν.
sentences.l:
but he struck the charioteer, the attendant,
the son of high-spirited Thebaeus, Eniopeus,
holding the reins of the horses, in the chest, by the breast.
sentences.i: but he struck Hector’s charioteer and attendant, Eniopeus, son of high-spirited Thebaeus, as he held the horses’ reins, in the chest beside the breast.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Diomedes (‘but he’), and the victim is named in the accusative Ἠνιοπῆα, with ἡνίοχον θεράποντα ‘charioteer, attendant’ in apposition. Θηβαίου is taken here as a man’s name, Thebaeus; it could also be read as the adjective ‘Theban’. ὑπερθύμου ‘high-spirited’ is the Odyssey’s word. ἔχοντα is ‘holding’, and στῆθος and μαζόν are the part struck, the chest beside the breast (μαζός is the male breast).

sentences.t:
ἤριπε δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων, ὑπερώησαν δέ οἱ ἵπποι
ὠκύποδες·
sentences.l:
and he fell out of the chariot, and swerved aside for him the horses,
swift-footed;
sentences.i: He fell from the chariot, and the swift-footed horses swerved aside;
sentences.n: ἤριπε is the aorist of ἐρείπω ‘fall headlong’, and ἐξ ὀχέων is ‘out of the chariot’. ὑπερώησαν is a rare verb, usually explained as ‘swerved, shied aside’, and οἱ is a dative ‘at him’. ὠκύποδες ‘swift-footed’ ‘swift-footed’, the stock epithet, is held over to the start of the next line.

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ αὖθι λύθη ψυχή τε μένος τε.
sentences.l: and of him on the spot was loosed the soul and the might.
sentences.i: and on the spot his soul and his might were loosed.
sentences.n: The formula for a man’s death: λύθη ‘was loosed’ (aorist passive of λύω) with the two subjects ψυχή ‘soul’ and μένος ‘might’, and the verb stays singular. τοῦ is ‘of him’ (Eniopeus), and αὖθι is ‘there, on the spot’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορα δ’ αἰνὸν ἄχος πύκασε φρένας ἡνιόχοιο·
sentences.l: And Hector fearsome grief covered about the wits, for his charioteer;
sentences.i: and fearsome grief covered Hector’s wits for his charioteer;
sentences.n: The grief is the subject: αἰνὸν ἄχος, ‘fearsome grief’, with the verb πύκασε, aorist of πυκάζω ‘cover thickly, wrap round’. Ἕκτορα … φρένας puts the person and the part in the accusative, ‘Hector, round the wits’, and ἡνιόχοιο is a genitive ‘for the charioteer’ saying what the grief is for.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἔπειτ’ εἴασε καὶ ἀχνύμενός περ ἑταίρου
κεῖσθαι,
sentences.l:
Him indeed then he allowed, though grieving for his companion,
to lie,
sentences.i: Then he let him lie, though he grieved for his companion,
sentences.n: Hector leaves the dead man where he fell. τὸν μέν is ‘him, for his part’, and εἴασε is the aorist of ἐάω ‘allow’, governing the infinitive κεῖσθαι ‘to lie’. ἀχνύμενός περ is ‘though grieving’ (περ gives the concession), and ἑταίρου is the genitive ‘for his companion’.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἡνίοχον μέθεπε θρασύν·
sentences.l: but he sought a charioteer, a bold one;
sentences.i: and went in search of a bold charioteer;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘but he’ is Hector, set against τὸν μέν in the unit before. μέθεπε is the imperfect of μετέπω ‘go after’, here ‘went after, sought out’. θρασύς is ‘bold’, and the unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτι δὴν
ἵππω δευέσθην σημάντορος·
sentences.l:
and not for long, then,
did the two horses lack a commander;
sentences.i: and the two horses were not left long without someone to command them;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτι δήν is ‘and not for long, then’. ἵππω is the dual ‘the two horses’ and δευέσθην is the dual of the imperfect passive of δεύομαι ‘lack’, which takes the genitive σημάντορος, ‘a commander’ (from σημαίνω ‘give a sign, direct’). The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
αἶψα γὰρ εὗρεν
Ἰφιτίδην Ἀρχεπτόλεμον θρασύν, ὅν ῥα τόθ’ ἵππων
ὠκυπόδων ἐπέβησε, δίδου δέ οἱ ἡνία χερσίν.
sentences.l:
for at once he found
Iphitus’-son Archeptolemus, bold, whom then of horses
swift-footed he made mount, and gave him the reins into his hands.
sentences.i: for at once he found bold Archeptolemus, son of Iphitus, and set him up behind the swift-footed horses and gave him the reins into his hands.
sentences.n: Hector finds a new charioteer. Ἰφιτίδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Iphitus’. ἐπέβησε is the transitive aorist of ἐπιβαίνω, ‘made mount’, taking the genitive ἵππων ὠκυπόδων (a team, by implication its chariot), so ‘put him in charge of the swift-footed horses’ in sense. δίδου is the imperfect ‘was giving’, and οἱ is ‘to him’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κε λοιγὸς ἔην καὶ ἀμήχανα ἔργα γένοντο,
καί νύ κε σήκασθεν κατὰ Ἴλιον ἠΰτε ἄρνες,
sentences.l:
Then would ruin have been, and deeds past help have come to pass,
and they would have been penned in Ilios like lambs,
sentences.i: Then there would have been ruin, and deeds past all remedy would have come to pass, and the Trojans would have been penned up in Ilios like lambs,
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and a ‘near thing’ sentence: κε with the imperfect ἔην (= ἦν) and the aorist γένοντο says what would have happened if Zeus had not seen; the condition follows in 132. λοιγός is ‘ruin’. ἀμήχανα are things with no ‘resource’ (μηχανή), so deeds one cannot deal with. σήκασθεν is the aorist passive of σηκάζω ‘pen in a fold’, with the Trojans understood as subject, and ἠΰτε is ‘like’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὀξὺ νόησε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε·
sentences.l: had not sharply noticed the father of men and of gods;
sentences.i: had the father of men and of gods not been quick to notice;
sentences.n: The condition left over from the unit before: εἰ μὴ … νόησε ‘if he had not noticed’. ὀξύ is the adverb ‘sharply’, and the father of men and of gods is Zeus without his name, the stock phrase. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: βροντήσας δ’ ἄρα δεινὸν ἀφῆκ’ ἀργῆτα κεραυνόν,
sentences.l: but thundering, he sent forth a dread, bright thunderbolt,
sentences.i: but he thundered and let loose a dread, bright thunderbolt,
sentences.n: βροντήσας is the aorist participle of βροντάω ‘thunder’, and ἀφῆκ’ is ἀφῆκε ‘let go’ with the vowel elided. δεινόν ‘dread’ and ἀργῆτα ‘bright’ (ἀργής) both qualify κεραυνόν ‘thunderbolt’, ἀργῆτα being the accusative of ἀργής ‘bright’, an old form with the stem in -ητ-.

sentences.t: κὰδ δὲ πρόσθ’ ἵππων Διομήδεος ἧκε χαμᾶζε·
sentences.l: and down in front of the horses of Diomedes he sent it to the ground;
sentences.i: and sent it down to the ground in front of Diomedes’ horses;
sentences.n: κὰδ … ἧκε is κατῆκε with the preposition split off (tmesis) and its final consonant assimilated to the δ of δέ, ‘sent down’. χαμᾶζε is ‘to the ground’ (the ending -ζε, like -δε, marks motion towards). The bolt falls in front of Diomedes’ team.

sentences.t: δεινὴ δὲ φλὸξ ὦρτο θεείου καιομένοιο,
sentences.l: and a dread flame rose of burning sulphur,
sentences.i: and a dread flame of burning sulphur rose up,
sentences.n: θεείου is the genitive of θέειον ‘sulphur’, and φλόξ is ‘flame’. ὦρτο is the aorist of ὄρνυμι, ‘rose’, and καιομένοιο is the epic genitive of the participle ‘burning’.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ ἵππω δείσαντε καταπτήτην ὑπ’ ὄχεσφι·
sentences.l: and the two horses, having feared, cowered down beneath the chariot;
sentences.i: and the two horses, in fear, cowered down beneath the chariot;
sentences.n: τὼ … ἵππω and καταπτήτην are duals; the verb is the aorist of καταπτήσσω ‘cower, crouch down’. ὑπ’ ὄχεσφι is ‘under the chariot’ (the ending -φι is an old form for the dative plural). The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: Νέστορα δ’ ἐκ χειρῶν φύγον ἡνία σιγαλόεντα,
sentences.l: and from Nestor’s hands fled the glossy reins,
sentences.i: and the glossy reins slipped from Nestor’s hands,
sentences.n: φύγον is the aorist of φεύγω ‘flee’, here of the reins running away from him. Νέστορα ἐκ χειρῶν puts the man in the accusative with ‘from the hands’, the idiom for ‘from the hands of Nestor’.

sentences.t: δεῖσε δ’ ὅ γ’ ἐν θυμῷ, Διομήδεα δὲ προσέειπε·
sentences.l: and he was afraid in his heart, and Diomedes he addressed:
sentences.i: and he was afraid in his heart, and spoke to Diomedes:
sentences.n: δεῖσε is the aorist of δείδω ‘fear’, and ὅ γ’ is ‘he, for his part’, Nestor. θυμῷ is ‘heart’ and προσέειπε is ‘addressed’. The speech follows.

sentences.t: Τυδεΐδη ἄγε δ’ αὖτε φόβον δ’ ἔχε μώνυχας ἵππους.
sentences.l: “Tydeus’-son, come, now again to flight hold the solid-hoofed horses.
sentences.i: “Son of Tydeus, come now, turn the solid-hoofed horses to flight.
sentences.n: Nestor’s speech begins; he wants to run. Τυδεΐδη is a vocative, ἄγε ‘come’, and αὖτε ‘again, now’. φόβον δ’ is φόβονδε, ‘to flight’ (-δε of motion), and ἔχε is the imperative ‘hold, keep’ the horses to that course. μώνυχας ἵππους is ‘solid-hoofed horses’, one hoof each, as opposed to cloven.

sentences.t: ἦ οὐ γιγνώσκεις ὅ τοι ἐκ Διὸς οὐχ ἕπετ’ ἀλκή;
sentences.l: Do you not know that from Zeus might does not follow you?
sentences.i: Do you not know that might from Zeus does not go with you?
sentences.n: ἦ οὐ is a question expecting the answer yes. ὅ τοι is ὅτι τοι, ‘that … for you’, and ἕπετ’ is ἕπεται ‘follows, goes along with’. ἀλκή is ‘might’ and ἐκ Διός ‘from Zeus’ names its giver. Nestor reads the thunderbolt as Zeus withholding help.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν γὰρ τούτῳ Κρονίδης Ζεὺς κῦδος ὀπάζει
σήμερον·
sentences.l:
For now to this man the son of Cronus, Zeus, grants glory
today;
sentences.i: For today Zeus, the son of Cronus, grants glory to this man;
sentences.n: τούτῳ ‘to this man’ is Hector, not named. Κρονίδης Ζεύς is ‘Zeus, son of Cronus’, and κῦδος is ‘glory’. ὀπάζει is the same verb as at line 103, ‘make follow’, here with glory as the thing he sends: he ‘grants’ it. μὲν γάρ is answered by the αὖτε in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὕστερον αὖτε καὶ ἡμῖν, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσι,
δώσει·
sentences.l:
later, in turn, to us too, if he is willing,
he will give it;
sentences.i: later, if he is willing, he will give it to us as well;
sentences.n: ὕστερον ‘later’ is set against σήμερον ‘today’, and αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks the turn of events. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσι is αἰ κε ἐθέλῃ, ‘if he is willing’ (epic subjunctive with -σι). δώσει ‘will give’ has ‘it’ (the glory) as its understood object.

sentences.t:
ἀνὴρ δέ κεν οὔ τι Διὸς νόον εἰρύσσαιτο
οὐδὲ μάλ’ ἴφθιμος, ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτερός ἐστι.
sentences.l:
but a man could in no way hold back the mind of Zeus,
not even a very mighty one, since he is by far stronger.”
sentences.i: but no man could hold back the mind of Zeus, however mighty, since Zeus is far stronger.”
sentences.n: The reason to retreat. εἰρύσσαιτο is the aorist optative middle of ἐρύω (εἰρύω), whose middle sense ‘hold back, ward off’ suits νόον, ‘mind’, so ‘check the plan of Zeus’; κεν with the optative says ‘could’. οὔ τι is ‘in no way’ and οὐδὲ μάλ’ ἴφθιμος ‘not even a very mighty one’. φέρτερος is ‘stronger’. Nestor’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.l: Him then answered Diomedes, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: Then Diomedes, good at the war-cry, answered him:
sentences.n: The reply formula, with ἠμείβετο ‘answered’ and Diomedes’ standing epithet βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’, an accusative of respect (‘in the shout’). A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε πάντα γέρον κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες·
sentences.l: “Yes indeed, all this, old man, according to what is fitting you have said;
sentences.i: “Yes indeed, old man, all this you have said as is fitting;
sentences.n: Diomedes agrees. ναὶ δή is ‘yes indeed’, and κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘according to what is fitting’ (μοῖρα, share, here due measure), the idiom for speaking properly. ἔειπες is the epic aorist of λέγω. Diomedes’ speech begins.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τόδ’ αἰνὸν ἄχος κραδίην καὶ θυμὸν ἱκάνει·
sentences.l: But this fearsome grief reaches my heart and spirit;
sentences.i: But this fearsome grief comes upon my heart and spirit;
sentences.n: ἀλλά marks the objection. αἰνὸν ἄχος is ‘fearsome grief’ and ἱκάνει is ‘comes upon, reaches’. κραδίη ‘heart’ and θυμός ‘spirit’ are the two seats of feeling, and the grief is shame at the thought of what Hector will say, as the next lines show.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ γάρ ποτε φήσει ἐνὶ Τρώεσσ’ ἀγορεύων·
sentences.l: for Hector some day will say, declaring among the Trojans:
sentences.i: for some day Hector will say, declaring among the Trojans:
sentences.n: φήσει ‘will say’ is the future of φημί. ἀγορεύων ‘declaring’ is the verb for speaking in an assembly (ἀγορεύω), here to the Trojans. ποτε is ‘some day’. What Hector will say is given in the next unit, a speech inside Diomedes’ speech, so it carries single quotation marks.

sentences.t: Τυδεΐδης ὑπ’ ἐμεῖο φοβεύμενος ἵκετο νῆας.
sentences.l: ‘Tydeus’-son, by me put to flight, came to the ships.’
sentences.i: ‘The son of Tydeus came to the ships, in flight from me.’
sentences.n: The imagined boast. φοβεύμενος is the epic form of φοβούμενος from φοβέομαι, which in battle means ‘be put to flight, flee’, and ὑπ’ ἐμεῖο is ‘by me’ (ἐμεῖο is the epic genitive of ἐγώ). ἵκετο is the aorist middle of ἱκνέομαι, ‘came to’. The whole unit is Hector’s imagined words.

sentences.t: ὥς ποτ’ ἀπειλήσει· τότε μοι χάνοι εὐρεῖα χθών.
sentences.l: So some day he will threaten; then for me may the wide earth gape.”
sentences.i: That is what he will threaten some day; then may the wide earth open for me.”
sentences.n: ὥς … ἀπειλήσει is ‘so he will threaten’ (the future of ἀπειλέω), and τότε μοι χάνοι is ‘then may it gape for me’: χάνοι is the aorist optative of χάσκω ‘gape’ in a wish. εὐρεῖα χθών is ‘the wide earth’. Diomedes’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.l: Him then answered the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor answered him:
sentences.n: The reply formula again, with Nestor’s name and epithet; ἱππότα is the epic nominative. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι Τυδέος υἱὲ δαΐφρονος, οἷον ἔειπες.
sentences.l: “Ah me, son of wise-minded Tydeus, what a thing you have said.
sentences.i: “Ah, son of wise-hearted Tydeus, what a thing you have said.
sentences.n: ὤ μοι is an exclamation, ‘ah me’. Τυδέος υἱέ is a vocative and δαΐφρονος ‘wise-minded’ belongs to Τυδέος, not to the vocative; whether δαΐφρων means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed, and ‘wise’ is the usual choice. οἷον is ‘what a (thing)’, an exclamatory relative, and ἔειπες is the aorist of λέγω. Nestor’s speech begins.

sentences.t: εἴ περ γάρ σ’ Ἕκτωρ γε κακὸν καὶ ἀνάλκιδα φήσει,
sentences.l: For even if Hector does call you base and without might,
sentences.i: For even if Hector says that you are base and lack might,
sentences.n: εἴ περ … φήσει is ‘even if he says’ (a condition with the future of φημί, ‘say’); φήσει takes two accusatives, σε … κακὸν καὶ ἀνάλκιδα, ‘you … base and without might’. ἀνάλκιδα is the accusative of ἄναλκις, built on ἀλκή ‘might’ with ἀν- ‘not’. κακός here is ‘base’, a man without worth.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐ πείσονται Τρῶες καὶ Δαρδανίωνες
καὶ Τρώων ἄλοχοι μεγαθύμων ἀσπιστάων,
τάων ἐν κονίῃσι βάλες θαλεροὺς παρακοίτας.
sentences.l:
yet they will not believe it, the Trojans and Dardanians
and the wives of the great-hearted Trojan shield-bearers,
whose flourishing consorts you cast down in the dust.”
sentences.i: yet the Trojans and Dardanians will not believe him, nor will the wives of the great-hearted Trojan shield-bearers, whose flourishing husbands you cast down in the dust.”
sentences.n: The answer to the condition. πείσονται is the future middle of πείθω, ‘will be persuaded, believe’. Δαρδανίωνες is a form of ‘Dardanians’, the same people as Δάρδανοι. μεγαθύμων ‘great-hearted’ and ἀσπιστάων (epic genitive plural of ἀσπιστής, ‘shield-bearer’) both agree with Τρώων. βάλες is the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω, ‘you cast down’; θαλεροὺς παρακοίτας are ‘flourishing husbands’ (παράκοιτις is ‘wife’, the masculine means ‘one who lies beside’). κονίῃσι is a plural form of ‘dust’. Nestor’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας φύγαδε τράπε μώνυχας ἵππους
αὖτις ἀν’ ἰωχμόν·
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, to flight he turned the solid-hoofed horses
back through the press of the fight;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and turned the solid-hoofed horses to flight, back through the press of the fight;
sentences.n: A new paragraph; Nestor is the subject, as the driver (116), and ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is ‘so, then, having spoken’. φύγαδε is ‘to flight’ and τράπε the aorist of τρέπω ‘turn’. ἰωχμός is a rare word for the crowd of the fight, and ‘press of the fight’ is a guess at its sense. The unit ends at the ano teleia. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δὲ Τρῶές τε καὶ Ἕκτωρ
ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ βέλεα στονόεντα χέοντο.
sentences.l:
and after him the Trojans and Hector
with wondrous din poured missiles full of groaning.
sentences.i: and after him the Trojans and Hector poured missiles that brought groaning, with a wondrous din.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … χέοντο is tmesis for ἐπεχέοντο, ‘poured upon’, with the middle voice ‘poured themselves forth’. ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ is ‘with wondrous din’ (θεσπέσιος ‘wondrous’). βέλεα is ‘missiles’; the poet does not say whether they are spears or arrows. στονόεντα ‘full of groaning’ means that they bring groans to those they strike.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ μακρὸν ἄϋσε μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: And at him he shouted loudly, great Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: And great Hector of the glancing helmet cried out loudly at him:
sentences.n: The speech introduction, with κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ (κόρυς ‘helmet’ + αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’) and μέγας ‘great’. τῷ … ἐπί is ‘after him, at him’ (the preposition follows its pronoun), and ἄϋσε is the aorist of ἀΰω ‘shout’. Hector is shouting at Diomedes’ back.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδη περὶ μέν σε τίον Δαναοὶ ταχύπωλοι
ἕδρῃ τε κρέασίν τε ἰδὲ πλείοις δεπάεσσι·
sentences.l:
“Tydeus’-son, above others honoured you the swift-colted Danaans
with a seat, and with meats, and with full cups;
sentences.i: “Son of Tydeus, the Danaans with their swift colts used to honour you above all others with a seat, with meats, and with full cups;
sentences.n: Hector’s taunt begins with what Diomedes used to be given. περὶ … τίον is ‘honoured exceedingly, above others’ (τίω, imperfect, ‘used to honour’), and Δαναοὶ ταχύπωλοι is ‘the Danaans with their swift colts’. ἕδρῃ τε κρέασίν τε is ‘with a seat and with meats’ and ἰδέ is ‘and’; πλείοις is the epic form of ‘full’, not the comparative ‘more’. Hector’s speech begins.

sentences.t: νῦν δέ σ’ ἀτιμήσουσι· γυναικὸς ἄρ’ ἀντὶ τέτυξο.
sentences.l: but now they will dishonour you; in place of a woman, then, you have been made.
sentences.i: but now they will dishonour you; you have turned out to be no better than a woman.
sentences.n: νῦν δέ sets the present against the past. ἀτιμήσουσι is the future of ἀτιμάζω ‘dishonour’. γυναικὸς ἀντί is ‘in place of a woman’, and τέτυξο is the perfect passive of τεύχω in the second person, ‘you have been made’. The sense is that Diomedes is no more than a woman.

sentences.t: ἔρρε κακὴ γλήνη,
sentences.l: Be gone, base doll,
sentences.i: Be off, you worthless doll,
sentences.n: ἔρρε is the imperative of ἔρρω ‘go away, go to ruin’. γλήνη means ‘doll’ (also the pupil of the eye), a girl’s plaything, here a gibe at a man who is no man. κακή is ‘worthless’ and agrees with γλήνη.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὐκ εἴξαντος ἐμεῖο
πύργων ἡμετέρων ἐπιβήσεαι,
sentences.l:
since, not with my yielding, our towers
you will mount,
sentences.i: since you will not mount our towers with my yielding,
sentences.n: οὐκ εἴξαντος ἐμεῖο is a genitive absolute, ‘I not having given way’ (aorist of εἴκω ‘give way’), and the negative covers the main verb: the sense is that Diomedes will not climb the walls while Hector holds. ἐπιβήσεαι is the future middle of ἐπιβαίνω ‘mount’, with the genitive πύργων ἡμετέρων ‘our towers’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γυναῖκας
ἄξεις ἐν νήεσσι·
sentences.l:
nor will you lead women
away in the ships;
sentences.i: nor will you carry off our women in your ships;
sentences.n: οὐδέ ‘nor’ continues the denial. ἄξεις is the future of ἄγω, ‘lead away’, the verb for taking captives, with γυναῖκας ‘women’; ἐν νήεσσι is ‘in ships’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: πάρος τοι δαίμονα δώσω.
sentences.l: before that, to you your destiny I shall give.”
sentences.i: I shall deal you your destiny before that.”
sentences.n: πάρος is ‘before (that)’. δαίμονα is a divine power; here it means the power that deals a man his lot, so ‘destiny’, and the threat is death at Hector’s hands. τοι is ‘to you’ and δώσω ‘I shall give’. Hector’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Τυδεΐδης δὲ διάνδιχα μερμήριξεν
ἵππους τε στρέψαι καὶ ἐναντίβιον μαχέσασθαι.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Tydeus’-son was in doubt between two courses,
to turn the horses and to fight face to face.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the son of Tydeus was in doubt between two courses, to turn his horses and to fight face to face.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. διάνδιχα μερμήριξεν is ‘was in doubt between two courses’, (διάνδιχα, ‘in two ways’). The infinitives name the first course, to turn the horses round, and to fight ἐναντίβιον, ‘face to face, in open conflict’; the other course, flight, is left unsaid. ἵππους … στρέψαι is the aorist infinitive of στρέφω ‘turn’, and μαχέσασθαι of μάχομαι ‘fight’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: τρὶς μὲν μερμήριξε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν,
sentences.l: Three times he pondered in mind and in heart,
sentences.i: Three times he pondered in his mind and heart,
sentences.n: τρίς ‘three times’. μερμήριξε is ‘pondered’, and κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in mind and in heart’. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
τρὶς δ’ ἄρ’ ἀπ’ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων κτύπε μητίετα Ζεὺς
σῆμα τιθεὶς Τρώεσσι μάχης ἑτεραλκέα νίκην.
sentences.l:
and three times from the Idaean mountains thundered Zeus the counsellor,
putting a sign for the Trojans, a victory in battle, other-strengthening.
sentences.i: and three times Zeus the counsellor thundered from the mountains of Ida, setting a sign for the Trojans, a victory in battle that turns the fight to the other side.
sentences.n: The thunder answers Diomedes’ three-fold doubt. τρὶς δ’ ἄρα ‘and three times’ matches τρὶς μέν. κτύπε is ‘thundered’ (κτυπέω), and μητίετα Ζεύς is ‘Zeus the counsellor’, μητίετα being an old nominative. Ἰδαίων ὀρέων is ‘the Idaean mountains’. σῆμα τιθείς is ‘setting a sign’ and the sign is a victory in battle that is ἑτεραλκέα, ‘strengthening the other side’ (ἕτερος + ἀλκή), that is, one that turns the fight.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δὲ Τρώεσσιν ἐκέκλετο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.l: And Hector to the Trojans called out, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: And Hector gave orders to the Trojans, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: ἐκέκλετο is the aorist middle of κέλομαι, ‘called, urged’; ἀΰσας is ‘shouting’ (aorist participle of ἀΰω), with μακρόν ‘loudly’. Hector answers the thunder with a speech to his men.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες καὶ Λύκιοι καὶ Δάρδανοι ἀγχιμαχηταὶ
ἀνέρες ἔστε φίλοι, μνήσασθε δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς.
sentences.l:
“Trojans and Lycians and Dardanians, close-fighters,
men be, friends, and be mindful of impetuous might,
sentences.i: “Trojans and Lycians and Dardanians, fighters at close quarters, be men, friends, and remember impetuous might,
sentences.n: A speech to the army and its allies. Λύκιοι are the Lycians; Δάρδανοι ‘Dardanians’. ἀγχιμαχηταί is ‘close-fighters’ (ἀγχί ‘near’ + μάχομαι). ἀνέρες ἔστε is ‘be men’, the call to courage. μνήσασθε is ‘be mindful, remember’, with the genitive ἀλκῆς, and θούριδος ‘impetuous’. Hector’s speech begins.

sentences.t:
γιγνώσκω δ’ ὅτι μοι πρόφρων κατένευσε Κρονίων
νίκην καὶ μέγα κῦδος, ἀτὰρ Δαναοῖσί γε πῆμα·
sentences.l:
And I know that, ready-minded, he nodded to me,
the son of Cronus, victory and great glory, and for the Danaans woe;
sentences.i: I know that the son of Cronus has nodded to me with a ready mind: victory and great glory for me, and woe for the Danaans;
sentences.n: γιγνώσκω ‘I know’ rests on the three claps of thunder. πρόφρων ‘ready-minded’ is ‘willingly’ in sense, and κατένευσε is the aorist of κατανεύω ‘nod assent’, a nod being a promise. Κρονίων is ‘son of Cronus’. νίκην καὶ μέγα κῦδος is ‘victory and great glory’; ἀτάρ … γε marks the contrast, ‘but for the Danaans at least’, and πῆμα is ‘woe’.

sentences.t:
νήπιοι οἳ ἄρα δὴ τάδε τείχεα μηχανόωντο
ἀβλήχρ’ οὐδενόσωρα·
sentences.l:
Foolish men, who these walls devised,
feeble, of no account;
sentences.i: Fools, who devised this wall, feeble and of no account!
sentences.n: νήπιοι ‘foolish’, followed by οἳ ἄρα δή, ‘who, as it seems’, marks the sneer at the Achaean wall. τείχεα is a plural for one wall; μηχανόωντο is the imperfect middle of μηχανάομαι ‘devise’. ἀβλήχρα is ‘feeble’ and οὐδενόσωρα ‘of no account’, a rare word whose second element is not clear. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: τὰ δ’ οὐ μένος ἁμὸν ἐρύξει·
sentences.l: but these will not hold back my might;
sentences.i: but they will not hold back my might;
sentences.n: τὰ δ’ ‘but these’ are the walls, a neuter plural subject with a singular verb ἐρύξει (future of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’), a regular Greek construction. μένος ‘might’ is the object. ἁμόν is a by-form of the possessive, ‘my’ or ‘our’; Hector speaks of his own strength.

sentences.t: ἵπποι δὲ ῥέα τάφρον ὑπερθορέονται ὀρυκτήν.
sentences.l: and the horses easily the ditch will leap over, the dug one.
sentences.i: and the horses will easily leap over the dug ditch.
sentences.n: ῥέα is ‘easily’, and ὑπερθορέονται is the future middle of ὑπερθρώσκω ‘leap over’ in epic form. τάφρον ὀρυκτήν is ‘the dug ditch’, ὀρυκτός being the adjective of ὀρύσσω ‘dig’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὅτε κεν δὴ νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσι γένωμαι,
sentences.l: But when indeed I shall have come to the hollow ships,
sentences.i: but when I have reached the hollow ships,
sentences.n: ὅτε κεν … γένωμαι is a future condition with the subjunctive, ‘when I shall have got’ to the ships. ἔπι is ἐπί placed after its noun, with the dative νηυσὶ γλαφυρῇσι ‘hollow ships’.

sentences.t: μνημοσύνη τις ἔπειτα πυρὸς δηΐοιο γενέσθω,
sentences.l: then let there be some remembrance of hostile fire,
sentences.i: let there then be some thought of hostile fire,
sentences.n: μνημοσύνη is ‘remembrance, mindfulness’, so ‘let someone remember the fire’: fire is wanted at the ships. γενέσθω is the third-person imperative of γίγνομαι, and πυρὸς δηΐοιο is ‘hostile fire’ (δήϊος ‘hostile’). The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
ὡς πυρὶ νῆας ἐνιπρήσω, κτείνω δὲ καὶ αὐτοὺς
Ἀργείους παρὰ νηυσὶν ἀτυζομένους ὑπὸ καπνοῦ.
sentences.l:
so that with fire I may burn the ships, and kill
the Argives themselves beside the ships, dazed with fear from the smoke.”
sentences.i: so that I may burn the ships with fire and kill the Argives themselves beside the ships, dazed with fear at the smoke.”
sentences.n: ὡς is ‘so that’ and ἐνιπρήσω is the subjunctive of ἐνιπίμπρημι ‘set on fire’; κτείνω is a short-vowel subjunctive too, ‘and I may kill’. Ἀργείους is ‘Argives’, another name for the Achaeans. ἀτυζομένους is ‘dazed with fear’, and ὑπὸ καπνοῦ is ‘from the smoke’. Hector’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἵπποισιν ἐκέκλετο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.l: So having spoken, to the horses he called out and lifted his voice:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and called out to his horses, raising his voice:
sentences.n: Hector now addresses his team. ἐκέκλετο is ‘called out’ (κέλομαι), and φώνησε ‘lifted his voice, spoke aloud’, so the two verbs make a doubled introduction. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
Ξάνθέ τε καὶ σὺ Πόδαργε καὶ Αἴθων Λάμπέ τε δῖε
νῦν μοι τὴν κομιδὴν ἀποτίνετον,
sentences.l:
“Xanthus, and you, Podargus, and Aethon, and heavenly Lampus,
now to me the tending repay,
sentences.i: “Xanthus, and you, Podargus, and Aethon, and heavenly Lampus, now repay me for the care
sentences.n: The four horses are called by name: Ξάνθος ‘Chestnut’ (ξανθός ‘yellow’), Πόδαργος (‘swift-foot’ or ‘white-foot’, since ἀργός can mean either), Αἴθων ‘Blazing’ and Λάμπος ‘Bright’. The edition prints the vocatives Ξάνθέ and Λάμπέ with an accent on the last syllable. δῖε is ‘heavenly’, as with men. ἀποτίνετον is the dual imperative ‘repay’ (ἀποτίνω), and κομιδήν is ‘care, tending’ (from κομέω). Hector’s speech begins.

sentences.t:
ἣν μάλα πολλὴν
Ἀνδρομάχη θυγάτηρ μεγαλήτορος Ἠετίωνος
ὑμῖν πὰρ προτέροισι μελίφρονα πυρὸν ἔθηκεν
οἶνόν τ’ ἐγκεράσασα πιεῖν, ὅτε θυμὸς ἀνώγοι,
sentences.l:
which, a very great one,
Andromache, daughter of great-spirited Eetion,
beside you earlier ones set, honey-hearted wheat,
and wine mixing in to drink, whenever your heart bade,
sentences.i: that Andromache, daughter of great-spirited Eetion, gave you first, setting heart-sweetening wheat before you and mixing in wine for you to drink whenever your heart bade,
sentences.n: The relative clause says what the care was: wheat and wine. ἣν … πολλήν is ‘which, very great’; πὰρ … ἔθηκεν is παρέθηκεν split (tmesis), ‘set beside, set before’. ὑμῖν … προτέροισι is ‘to you, the earlier ones’: the horses were fed before Hector. μελίφρονα is ‘heart-sweetening’, whose second element makes the exact sense uncertain, and πυρόν is ‘wheat’. ἐγκεράσασα is ‘mixing in’, and ὅτε θυμὸς ἀνώγοι is ‘whenever the heart bade’ (a general case, with the optative).

sentences.t: ἢ ἐμοί, ὅς πέρ οἱ θαλερὸς πόσις εὔχομαι εἶναι.
sentences.l: or than me, who claim to be her flourishing husband.
sentences.i: before me, who claim to be her flourishing husband.
sentences.n: ἢ ἐμοί finishes the comparison started by προτέροισι: ‘earlier than to me’. ὅς πέρ … εὔχομαι εἶναι is ‘I who claim to be’ (εὔχομαι ‘claim’), with θαλερὸς πόσις ‘flourishing husband’. The horses come before the husband in Andromache’s care, which is the point of the reminder.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐφομαρτεῖτον καὶ σπεύδετον ὄφρα λάβωμεν
ἀσπίδα Νεστορέην,
sentences.l:
But follow closely and hasten, so that we may take
the shield of Nestor,
sentences.i: But keep close behind and hurry, so that we may take Nestor’s shield,
sentences.n: The horses are told to hurry. ἐφομαρτεῖτον and σπεύδετον are duals of the imperative, ‘you two follow closely’ and ‘hasten’ (σπεύδω). ὄφρα λάβωμεν is a purpose clause, ‘so that we may take’. Νεστορέην is the adjective ‘of Nestor’ and agrees with ἀσπίδα ‘shield’.

sentences.t:
τῆς νῦν κλέος οὐρανὸν ἵκει
πᾶσαν χρυσείην ἔμεναι, κανόνας τε καὶ αὐτήν,
sentences.l:
of which now the fame reaches heaven,
to be all of gold, the rods and the shield itself,
sentences.i: whose fame now reaches heaven, that it is wholly of gold, its rods and the shield itself,
sentences.n: τῆς … κλέος is ‘of which the fame’, and οὐρανὸν ἵκει is ‘reaches heaven’. The fame says (the infinitive ἔμεναι, ‘to be’, is the epic form) that it is πᾶσαν χρυσείην ‘all golden’. κανόνας are ‘rods’, the bars of a shield, whose exact function (handles or cross-bars) is not certain. τε καὶ αὐτήν is ‘and the shield itself’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἀπ’ ὤμοιιν Διομήδεος ἱπποδάμοιο
δαιδάλεον θώρηκα, τὸν Ἥφαιστος κάμε τεύχων.
sentences.l:
but from the two shoulders of Diomedes, horse-taming,
the cunningly wrought breastplate, which Hephaestus toiled at making.
sentences.i: and from the shoulders of Diomedes, tamer of horses, the cunningly wrought breastplate that Hephaestus toiled to make.
sentences.n: The second prize. ἀπ’ ὤμοιιν is ‘from the two shoulders’, a dual genitive, and ἱπποδάμοιο ‘tamer of horses’ is Diomedes’ epithet here. δαιδάλεον is ‘cunningly wrought’ and θώρηκα ‘breastplate’. κάμε τεύχων is ‘toiled at making’ (the aorist of κάμνω with a participle of τεύχω). αὐτάρ ‘and then’ goes on with what Hector wants.

sentences.t:
εἰ τούτω κε λάβοιμεν, ἐελποίμην κεν Ἀχαιοὺς
αὐτονυχὶ νηῶν ἐπιβησέμεν ὠκειάων.
sentences.l:
If we could take these two, I would hope that the Achaeans
in this very night would board the swift ships.”
sentences.i: If we could take these two, I should hope that this very night the Achaeans would board their swift ships.”
sentences.n: τούτω is the dual ‘these two’, the shield and the breastplate. εἰ … κε λάβοιμεν is a wish-condition (optative), and ἐελποίμην κεν is ‘I should hope’ (ἐέλπομαι = ἔλπομαι). ἐπιβησέμεν is the future infinitive (epic -μεν) of ἐπιβαίνω with the genitive νηῶν ὠκειάων ‘swift ships’, the sense ‘embark’. αὐτονυχί is ‘that very night’, a rare word. Hector’s speech ends here.
